bill.title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States relating to the authority of Congress and the States to regulate contributions and expenditures intended to affect elections and to enact public financing systems for political campaigns.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The amendment would directly regulate how advocacy organizations raise and spend money to influence elections.
The amendment would reshape campaign-finance law and likely generate substantial litigation and compliance work for law firms and lobbying practices.
Regulations on election-related spending could affect advertising revenue and the market for political communications services.
New restrictions on corporate election spending and potential public financing systems could affect financial institutions' political engagement and compliance obligations.

bill.plainSummary: This proposed constitutional amendment would allow Congress and state legislatures to set limits on how much money candidates and others can raise and spend to influence elections. It would also permit them to create public financing systems for campaigns and to treat corporations differently from individual people, including by prohibiting corporations from spending money on elections. The amendment would give lawmakers the authority to write laws implementing these changes.

bill.title: To reauthorize the Young Women’s Breast Health Education and Awareness Requires Learning Young Act of 2009.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

industries.rationale: The bill funds screening, diagnostic, and treatment services that hospitals and health systems deliver to low-income patients.
The bill supports diagnostic testing and treatment services for breast and cervical cancer, which involve medical devices and pharmaceuticals.
The program targets uninsured individuals, potentially affecting the pool of patients who might otherwise seek coverage or remain uninsured.

bill.plainSummary: This bill extends federal funding through 2030–2031 for Centers for Disease Control and Prevention programs that help low-income and uninsured women access breast and cervical cancer screening and treatment. It gives states more flexibility in how they spend grant money and requires a government report on how many people are served and what barriers prevent access. The bill also continues education campaigns and research focused on breast cancer in younger women.

plain.whoItTouches: People with cancer, and the people caring for them.

bill.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
bill.latestActionText: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 466.
subjects: Department of Health and Human Services

industries.rationale: The bill directly funds research grants and regulatory pathways for development of drugs and therapies targeting ALS and neurodegenerative diseases.
Providers treating ALS patients may see changes in available investigational therapies and clinical trial access, though the bill focuses primarily on research and regulatory processes.

bill.plainSummary: This bill extends funding through fiscal year 2031 for federal programs that support research and development of treatments for ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease) and similar neurodegenerative diseases. It requires the National Institutes of Health to track safety data on experimental drugs and mandates that the Food and Drug Administration publish a five-year plan describing how it will help develop and approve therapies for these rare diseases. The bill also continues a public-private partnership between federal agencies and outside organizations working on neurodegenerative disease treatments.

plain.whoItTouches: People with an illness that is still being studied. Anyone who uses the internet.

bill.title: To clarify the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016, to appropriately limit the application of defenses based on the passage of time and other non-merits defenses to claims under that Act.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
subjects: War crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity

industries.rationale: The bill expands litigation procedures, jurisdictional reach, and limits defenses in civil claims, directly affecting law firms handling art recovery and international litigation.
Museums and cultural institutions holding artwork are subject to expanded liability and jurisdictional reach under the modified claims procedures.

bill.plainSummary: This bill removes the 2026 deadline for filing lawsuits to recover art and property stolen during the Holocaust, allowing claims to be filed indefinitely as long as they are brought within six years of discovering the item. It makes it easier to sue foreign governments in U.S. courts and to serve legal papers on defendants anywhere in the country. The bill also blocks certain legal defenses, such as arguments that too much time has passed or that U.S. courts should defer to foreign laws, for both current and future cases.

plain.whoItTouches: People who have been the victim of a crime.

bill.title: Washington, D.C. Admission Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, and in addition to the Committees on Rules, Armed Services, the Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.
subjects: Presidents and presidential powers, Vice Presidents

industries.rationale: The bill fundamentally restructures the governance of the District, creating a new state government and redefining the federal district.
Statehood would change property tax authority and land-use regulation for most of the current District, affecting developers and property owners.
The transition of DC courts, judicial proceedings, and contractual obligations to state authority would affect legal practice and litigation in the new jurisdiction.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would admit most of the current District of Columbia as the 51st state, called Washington, Douglass Commonwealth, with two senators and one representative in Congress. A small federal district containing the Capitol, White House, Supreme Court, and nearby monuments would remain as the seat of the federal government. The bill sets up a transition process for DC laws, courts, contracts, and obligations to continue under state authority, and creates a commission to manage the shift to statehood.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who votes.

bill.title: SEED Act
bill.latestActionText: Cloture motion on the motion to proceed to the measure presented in Senate. (CR S4253)

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects early childhood education providers by changing the tax treatment of their employees' expenses.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would allow early childhood educators (pre-kindergarten teachers and staff) to claim the same federal tax deduction for unreimbursed classroom and professional development expenses that is currently available only to kindergarten through grade 12 educators. The deduction is capped at $300 in 2025 and adjusts annually for inflation. It would reduce taxable income for eligible early childhood educators who pay out-of-pocket for supplies and training.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who files a tax return. Anyone who pays federal tax.

bill.title: Safe Schools Improvement Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

industries.rationale: The bill imposes new policy, reporting, and grievance-procedure obligations on local educational agencies and state education systems.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require states to ensure that local school districts adopt policies prohibiting bullying and harassment of students based on race, color, national origin, disability, religion, sex (including sexual orientation, gender identity, and intersex traits). School districts would need to notify students and parents annually about these policies, establish complaint procedures, and publicly report data on bullying incidents. The Department of Education would evaluate anti-bullying programs every two years, and the National Center for Education Statistics would collect nationwide data on these incidents.

plain.whoItTouches: School districts, and children in them. Children, and the adults responsible for them.

bill.title: Scientific Integrity Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.

industries.rationale: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies conduct and rely on federally funded research subject to these integrity requirements.
Federal research on climate, emissions, and energy impacts this sector's regulatory environment and public discourse.
Federal research on energy technologies and climate directly affects this sector's market and policy landscape.
Agricultural research conducted or funded by USDA and other agencies would be subject to these integrity standards.
Universities receive federal research funding and would need to comply with integrity policies in their federally supported work.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require every federal agency that funds, conducts, or oversees scientific research to create and enforce a policy protecting scientific integrity. These policies must ensure that research conclusions are not influenced by political considerations, prohibit suppression or alteration of findings, and allow researchers to share their work. Each agency would need to appoint a Scientific Integrity Officer, establish a complaint process, provide training, and submit its policy to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy for approval.

bill.title: PRECISE Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology.

industries.rationale: The bill directly expands USDA loan and conservation programs to fund precision agriculture equipment and practices for crop and livestock producers.
The bill creates new federal support for precision agriculture technology and equipment, expanding the market for sensors, software, and data systems used in farming.
The bill would increase demand for precision agriculture equipment such as GPS-guided machinery, variable-rate applicators, and monitoring devices.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would expand several USDA programs to support precision agriculture—technologies and practices that help farmers use seeds, fertilizer, water, and other inputs more efficiently. It would allow conservation loans, environmental quality incentives, and stewardship programs to fund precision agriculture equipment and practices. The bill would also direct USDA to use third-party providers for technical assistance on soil health and nutrient management.

plain.whoItTouches: Farmers, and anyone who buys food.

bill.title: Keeping All Students Safe Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce, and in addition to the Committee on Armed Services, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates schools and Head Start programs, imposing new training, compliance, and procedural obligations on educational institutions.
State educational agencies must establish and enforce new policies, and federal agencies administer grants and withhold payments for noncompliance.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would prohibit schools and Head Start programs that receive federal funding from confining students alone in locked rooms (seclusion) and would restrict the use of physical restraints to situations where a student poses an imminent danger of serious physical injury. It requires staff training in crisis intervention, establishes reporting procedures after restraint incidents, and allows students to sue if they are unlawfully restrained or secluded. States must create enforcement policies, and federal agencies can withhold payments from programs that violate the rules; a grant program would help states implement these requirements.

plain.whoItTouches: Students, teachers, and the families paying for it.

bill.title: Complete Streets Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

industries.rationale: The bill creates new federal grant programs and design standards that would generate demand for street reconstruction and infrastructure projects.
State and local governments would receive federal highway funds and face new obligations to establish grant programs, adopt policies, and implement design standards.
New design requirements for transit accommodation and multi-modal travel would affect how transportation providers operate and plan routes.
Requirements for specific street infrastructure like protected bike lanes, signalization, and lighting equipment would affect manufacturers of these products.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require states to create grant programs that help local governments, tribes, and planning organizations redesign roads to safely accommodate pedestrians, cyclists, transit users, and drivers of all ages and abilities. States and metropolitan planning organizations would need to adopt new design standards for sidewalks, crosswalks, protected bike lanes, and accessible features. The Department of Transportation would set benchmarks and phase in these "complete streets" standards for federally funded projects, with some exemptions.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who travels, by any means.

bill.title: GOSAFE Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The bill directly prohibits the manufacture, sale, import, and transfer of specific categories of firearms and ammunition devices.
Retailers selling firearms and ammunition would face new restrictions on what products they can legally stock and sell.
State and local governments would gain authority to use federal grant funds for buy-back programs and would enforce new criminal penalties.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would prohibit the import, sale, manufacture, transfer, and possession of gas-operated semiautomatic firearms and large-capacity ammunition magazines, with criminal penalties including fines and up to 12 months in prison for violations. Individuals possessing these firearms during a federal felony would face a mandatory minimum two-year sentence. The bill would allow state and local governments to use federal grant funds to operate buy-back programs for these firearms and magazines.

plain.whoItTouches: People caught up in the criminal law, and victims of crime.
